related_questions.question: How accurate are at-home COVID tests?

text_blocks.snippet: At-home COVID-19 antigen tests are generally accurate when detecting positive results, but they can be less accurate when identifying negative results, particularly early in an infection or in people without symptoms. While positive results are considered reliable, negative results may be inaccurate, especially if symptoms are present or after close contact with a positive individual.

list.title: Positive results are generally accurate:
list.snippet: Antigen tests detect the presence of viral proteins. If an at-home test shows a positive result, it's highly likely that the individual has COVID-19.

list.title: Negative results can be less accurate:
list.snippet: At-home tests can sometimes miss an infection, especially in the early stages or when someone is asymptomatic. This is known as a "false negative".

list.title: Factors affecting accuracy:
list.snippet: The accuracy of an at-home test can be affected by how well the test is performed, the timing of the test in relation to symptom onset, and the individual's viral load.

list.title: When to be cautious:
list.snippet: If you have symptoms of COVID-19, have been exposed to someone who tested positive, or if a negative result feels questionable, it's best to follow up with a PCR test (which is generally more sensitive) or consult with a healthcare professional, according to UCHealth, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention | CDC (.gov), and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (.gov).
